newsitem.title: USA: Lincoln buying CIGNA unit for $1.4 billion.
newsitem.headline: Lincoln buying CIGNA unit for $1.4 billion.

text.p: Lincoln National Corp. said on Monday it will buy CIGNA Corp.'s individual life insurance and annuity business for about $1.4 billion in cash.
Lincoln National said the deal, which is subject to regulatory approvals and is expected to close by year-end, should add to its 1998 earnings immediately.
Fort Wayne, Ind.-based Lincoln National said it expects increased sales from the combined businesses and expects to realise pretax expense savings of $40 million by 1999.

CIGNA, based in Philadelphia, said it expects to use the proceeds from the sale of the business to repurchase its stock. However, the company said it also may use the proceeds for internal growth or acquisitions.

"This transaction will bring together CIGNA's premier individual life insurance operations with Lincoln Life's leading annuity business to create one of the most powerful financial planning organisations in the country," Lincoln National Chief Executive Ian Rolland said in a statement.
The sale may mean CIGNA also wants to sell its property-casualty insurance business, analysts said.

"It kind of signals in their corporate decision-making process an interest in focusing on health care and employee benefit type transactions, which has got to raise the questions is (property-casualty) a keeper," said Weston Hicks, an analyst with Sanford C. Bernstein.
CIGNA bought Healthsource Inc., a New Hampshire based health maintenance organisation, last month for $1.7 billion including repayment of debt.

Lincoln National in June agreed to sell its 83.3 percent stake in American States Financial Corp., a property-casualty business, as it increased its focus on its life insurance, annuities and mutual funds businesses.
The sale of that business is expected to produce proceeds of $2.15 billion after tax.

Lincoln National said under the latest transaction it will receive the assets and liabilities of the acquired businesses while CIGNA will retain a surplus from the businesses that at the end of 1996 was about $225 million.
Lincoln National will reduce its dependence on its annuity business and strengthen its position in life insurance, said Mark Puccia, director of Standard & Poor's insurance rating services.
Although "Lincoln National paid a healthy price for this acquisition, they did at least invest in a line of business that makes a lot of sense for them," Puccia said.
Operations will continue in both Fort Wayne and the Hartford, Conn., area, where CIGNA's Individual Insurance business has its headquarters.

Lincoln National said the transaction will bring CIGNA Financial Advisors, which has 600 agents, a life brokerage operation and an annuity distribution system as well as about $37 billion of individual life insurance in force.
CIGNA's corporate-ownensurance, group life insurance, and life, health and accident reinsurance businesses are not part of the transaction.
"We believe this is an attractive transaction for CIGNA and its shareholders," CIGNA Chief Executive Wilson Taylor said in a statement.
"The individual life insurance and annuity operation is a strong business with solid returns, but has limited strategic connection to our other businesses," he said.
"The sale of this business, combined with our recent acquisition of Healthsource, an HMO and health insurance company, will strengthen our financial and strategic position," he said.
Lincon National stock closed at $67 a share, down 44 cents, and CIGNA closed at $196.94, up $5.94, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
